titre: Philippa Foot's Tram (1967): An Abortion Problem
accroche: The “trolley problem” appears in 1967 in an essay on abortion. There, the driver is not used to count lives but to test a doctrine.
contenu_vulgarise:
The driver of a runaway tram can only steer it from one narrow track onto another. Five men are working on one, a single man on the other, and whoever is on the track chosen will be killed. This scenario comes from an essay by the philosopher Philippa Foot, published in 1967 in the Oxford Review, a journal edited at University College, Oxford. Its title: “The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect.” The tram is introduced in a few lines, on page 8, in an eleven-page text.

## What the Essay Is After

Foot is interested in a doctrine that Catholics invoke in connection with abortion. It distinguishes what one aims at, as an end or as a means, from what one foresees without aiming at it: a “direct” intention and an “oblique” intention, in a vocabulary she borrows from Bentham. According to the doctrine, it is sometimes permissible to bring about by oblique intention what one would not have the right to aim at directly.

The controversy, Foot writes, has raged around specific cases, because the doctrine's opponents often seemed committed to indefensible views. The tram is one of them: the driver who steers toward the lone man foresees his death without aiming at it. By contrast, a judge facing a riot might have an innocent man executed to avert a bloodbath, the mob holding five hostages. Here the innocent man's death is necessary to his plan. Foot asks why we say without hesitation that the driver must steer, whereas most of us would be horrified by the idea of framing a culprit.

## An Answer Other Than the One You Expect

The doctrine of double effect offers an explanation, and Foot writes that she once found these arguments conclusive. She finally settles on a different solution. What matters, she says, is not the difference between aiming and foreseeing, but the one between avoiding harm and giving aid. The driver faces a conflict of negative duties: he must avoid injuring five men and avoid injuring one, he cannot do both, and he must cause the lesser harm. The judge, for his part, weighs the duty not to harm against the duty to help. Since we do not in general have the same duty to help as to refrain from harming, one cannot conclude from the one to the other.

In other words, with numbers equal, the judge has no right to have an innocent man hanged, and the driver must choose the less occupied track. Foot concludes that the distinction between direct and oblique intention plays a “quite subsidiary” role (p. 13). She also takes care to say that she has not shown that there are no other principles.

## A Name from Elsewhere

The expression “trolley problem” is not Foot's; she writes tram. It appears in the title of an article by Judith Jarvis Thomson, “Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem” (The Monist, 1976), then in “The Trolley Problem” (Yale Law Journal, 1985). Foot, moreover, introduces it after an airplane pilot about to crash, who decides to steer the aircraft toward a less inhabited area, placed beside the judge: to make the parallel with the judge as close as possible, she replaces the pilot with a tram driver. The question one readily associates with the tram, should we save the greatest number, is not hers: she answers with duties.

She herself specifies that in many cases it is very difficult to know what to say (p. 14). What, in those cases, decides between harming and failing to help?

repere.source: Philippa Foot, “The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect,” Oxford Review, 5, 1967, pp. 5-15

carte.punch: Foot's tram (1967) tests a doctrine about abortion, not just a calculation of lives.
carte.idee: Foot does not decide by numbers alone: the driver chooses between two harms, whereas the judge would harm one to help others. The difference between aiming and foreseeing, she writes, plays a “quite subsidiary” role.

quiz.question: According to Foot, why can the driver steer toward the lone man while the judge cannot have an innocent man executed?
choix: Because one need only count lives, and the judge simply makes a calculation error
Because the judge aims at the innocent man's death whereas the driver merely foresees it
Because the judge's act corrupts justice, which alone explains the whole difference
Because the driver chooses between two harms, whereas the judge would harm in order to give aid
quiz.explication: For Foot, the driver faces a conflict of negative duties and must do the lesser harm; the judge would be setting the duty not to harm against the duty to help, which is less strict. The second answer is the doctrine of double effect, whose distinction she says plays a “quite subsidiary” role. The third: she considers the corruption of justice very important, but the horror remains if a mere private individual frames the culprit. As for calculation, with numbers equal it would give the same answer in both cases.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which doctrine does Philippa Foot examine in her 1967 essay on abortion?
choix: The doctrine of double effect, which distinguishes direct intention from oblique intention
The doctrine of the lesser evil, which authorizes any act that reduces the total number of deaths
The doctrine of self-defense, invoked to justify harm done to an aggressor
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Foot is interested in a doctrine invoked by Catholics in connection with abortion, which distinguishes what one aims at as an end or as a means, direct intention, from what one foresees without aiming at it, oblique intention, a vocabulary she borrows from Bentham. The other two doctrines are not named in the entry.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the essay, through which figure does Foot first introduce a dilemma close to the tram's, before replacing it?
choix: A doctor who must choose between saving the mother or the child in a difficult delivery
An airplane pilot about to crash, who decides to steer the aircraft toward a less inhabited area
A ship's captain who must decide to throw part of the cargo overboard to save the crew
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that Foot introduces the tram after an airplane pilot about to crash, whom she replaces with a tram driver so that the parallel with the judge's case is as close as possible. The doctor and the captain do not appear in the essay as the entry reports it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the expression “trolley problem” come from, if not from Philippa Foot?
choix: From a logic textbook of the 1950s, predating Foot's essay
From Judith Jarvis Thomson, who uses it in articles from 1976 and then 1985
From a US Supreme Court ruling citing Foot's essay
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry indicates that Foot writes tram, and that the expression “trolley problem” appears in the title of an article by Judith Jarvis Thomson in 1976, then in a second one in 1985. The logic textbook and the Supreme Court ruling are not mentioned in the entry.
